# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Adaptive MCMC commonly calibrates a sampling-kernel parameter by Robbins--Monro stochastic approximation [@RobbinsMonro1951; @AndrieuThoms2008]. For example, a proposal scale can be adjusted using an acceptance-rate residual relative to a prescribed target. With the parameter frozen at $\theta$, the stationary expectation of that residual defines a field $h(\theta)$; the intended calibration equation is $h(\theta)=0$. More generally, adaptation seeks a root of a prescribed stationary mean-field equation.

Adam replaces the ordinary innovation by a nonlinear function of exponentially weighted first- and second-moment estimates. The memory coefficients are fixed, while the parameter gain decreases. Linear momentum preserves the frozen mean field in expectation, but Adam's random normaliser is coupled to its numerator. Its stationary field $F(\theta)$ need not coincide with $h(\theta)$, and the two calibration equations need not have the same roots.

Identifying this stationary field, proving that the actual stochastic recursion tracks an ODE, and proving convergence to a particular equilibrium are distinct questions. An ODE approximation with field $F$ does not establish convergence to a root of $h$, or even convergence to a single equilibrium of $F$. Dereich--Jentzen--Kassing [@Dereich2025_UJMNX8NK, Definition 1.3 and Theorem 1.5] identify the Adam field and establish an ODE approximation under IID innovations, with moment, regularity and gain assumptions and $\alpha^2<\beta<1$. Their analysis provides the IID benchmark; it does not supply the corresponding result for parameter-controlled Markov observations.

In adaptive MCMC the innovations are dependent and their transition law changes with the adaptation parameter. Freezing that parameter gives a homogeneous Markov driver. This note identifies the stationary calibration issue for that frozen system and constructs its stationary Adam memories. Augmenting the driver with these memories yields a Markov iterated function system (MIFS), with the transition structure in [@Fuh2021, equations (1.1) and (2.1)]. An argument based on stationary time reversal establishes a unique augmented invariant law under moment assumptions; the measure-level proof is retained in [Appendix A](#sec-appendix-fuh).

We then consider the stronger quantitative structure needed for stochastic approximation. A geometric coupling estimate for the driver, together with contractive memory and regularity of its forcing, yields Wasserstein contraction of the augmented kernel. This permits the perturbation theory of [@RudolfSchweizer2018, Theorem 3.1] to be applied to the parameter-indexed invariant laws, and the Poisson theory of [@Hofstadler2026] to be applied to Lipschitz observables. The assumptions are stated at the level of the driver and the memory update. The resulting stationary and parameter-regularity estimates are separate from the final adaptive ODE approximation, for which additional Poisson and stochastic-approximation conditions are identified but not inferred merely from frozen ergodicity.

The covariance identity remains the calibration question motivating these constructions. We distinguish the weaker assumptions sufficient to define that covariance from the additional contraction and parameter-regularity assumptions used to study the controlled recursion.
